question: Which statement correctly describes the particles in a gas?
options: Closely packed in a regular arrangement, vibrating in fixed positions
Close together but able to move past each other
Far apart, moving randomly at high speed
correct: Far apart, moving randomly at high speed

question: A block has a mass of 600 g and a volume of 200 cm³. What is its density?
What happens to the temperature of a substance during a change of state?
What is latent heat?
options: The energy needed to raise temperature by 1°C
The energy needed to change state without changing temperature
The energy stored in chemical bonds
The heat lost to the surroundings
correct: The energy needed to change state without changing temperature

question: What is absolute zero?
options: 0°C — the temperature at which water freezes

question: A gas is compressed at constant temperature. What happens to its pressure?
What is Brownian motion evidence for?
options: The particle model — that matter is made of small moving particles
The law of conservation of energy
correct: The particle model — that matter is made of small moving particles

question: Which change of state requires the most energy per kilogram for water?
A gas has a pressure of 100 kPa at 300 K. What is its pressure at 600 K if volume is constant?
What does internal energy include?
options: Only the kinetic energy of particles
Only the potential energy of particles
Both the kinetic and potential energy of all particles
The temperature of the substance only
correct: Both the kinetic and potential energy of all particles

question: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease with altitude?
options: The air gets warmer at higher altitudes
There is less air above so less weight pushing down
Gas particles move faster at higher altitudes
The volume of air increases at altitude
correct: There is less air above so less weight pushing down

question: Which change of state describes a solid turning directly into a gas?
Why do objects float on water if their density is less than 1000 kg/m³?
options: Their density is less than water so the upthrust exceeds their weight
Water pushes them up because it is moving
correct: Their density is less than water so the upthrust exceeds their weight

question: Which substance requires the most energy to heat by 1°C per kilogram?
Which temperature scale must be used in gas law calculations?
Density = mass ÷ __________.
The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing temperature is called specific __________ heat.
Absolute zero is __________ degrees Celsius.
To convert Celsius to Kelvin, you add __________ to the Celsius value.
The random motion of particles in a fluid, observed as the jiggling of pollen grains, is called __________ motion.
When a gas cools and turns into a liquid, this change of state is called __________.
The total kinetic and potential energy of all particles in a substance is called __________ energy.
At constant temperature, if the volume of a gas decreases, its pressure __________.
The change of state from solid directly to gas is called __________.
Density is measured in kg/m³ or __________.
Match each state of matter to its correct particle description.

pairs.definition: Particles in fixed positions, vibrating, closely packed in regular arrangement
Particles close together, able to move past each other, no fixed positions
Particles far apart, moving randomly at high speed, no fixed positions

question: Match each change of state to its correct description.
Match each gas law to its correct statement.

pairs.definition: At constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume
At constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature

question: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.definition: Energy to melt or freeze 1 kg of a substance
Energy to evaporate or condense 1 kg of a substance
Energy absorbed or released during a change of state

question: Match each material to whether it would float or sink in water (density 1000 kg/m³).

pairs.definition: Floats — density slightly less than water
Sinks — density much greater than water

question: State the equation for density.
mark_scheme: Density = mass ÷ volume / ρ = m/V (1).

question: State what is meant by absolute zero.
mark_scheme: The lowest possible temperature (1); −273°C or 0 K (1) — accept either.

question: A stone has a mass of 150 g and a volume of 50 cm³. Calculate its density.
State what happens to the temperature of a substance during a change of state.
mark_scheme: Temperature remains constant during a change of state (1).

question: Explain why the pressure of a gas increases when it is heated at constant volume.
mark_scheme: Particles move faster when heated (1); collide more frequently and with greater force with container walls (1); greater force per unit area means higher pressure (1) — any two.

question: Explain what Brownian motion is and what it tells us about matter.
mark_scheme: Random motion of small visible particles (e.g. pollen / smoke) (1); caused by collisions with smaller invisible molecules (1); provides evidence for the particle model (1) — any two.

question: Calculate the energy needed to melt 500 g of ice. The specific latent heat of fusion of water is 334 000 J/kg.
Describe how you would measure the density of an irregularly shaped stone in the laboratory.
mark_scheme: Measure the mass using a balance (1); measure volume by displacement — submerge in water and measure the volume of water displaced (1); calculate density = mass ÷ volume (1) — any two.

question: Explain why the temperature does not change while a substance is melting, even though energy is being supplied.
mark_scheme: Energy is used to break bonds between particles (1); not to increase kinetic energy / temperature (1); energy is stored as increased potential energy (1) — any two.

question: Explain, using the particle model, why a gas exerts pressure on the walls of its container.
mark_scheme: Gas particles move randomly at high speed (1); they collide with the walls of the container (1); each collision exerts a small force on the wall (1); the total force per unit area is the pressure (1) — any three.

question: Describe how you would measure the specific heat capacity of water in the lab.
mark_scheme: Heat known mass of water using an immersion heater (1); measure temperature change with thermometer (1); measure energy supplied using joulemeter or calculate E = Pt (1); use E = mcΔT to calculate c (1); insulate container to reduce energy losses (1) — any three.

question: Use the particle model to explain the differences in density between solids, liquids and gases.
mark_scheme: Solids have particles closely packed in regular arrangement (1); so high density (1); gases have particles far apart (1); so very low density (1); liquids are between solids and gases in density (1) — any three.

question: A sealed syringe contains gas at a pressure of 100 kPa and a volume of 60 cm³. The plunger is pushed in to reduce the volume to 20 cm³ at constant temperature. Calculate the new pressure and explain why it increases.
mark_scheme: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → 100 × 60 = P₂ × 20 (1); P₂ = 300 kPa (1); pressure increases because same number of particles in smaller volume (1); particles collide more frequently with walls (1).

question: Sketch and explain what a temperature-time graph would look like when a pure substance is heated from solid to gas at a constant rate.
mark_scheme: Temperature rises as solid is heated (1); flat section at melting point — temperature constant while melting (1); temperature rises again as liquid is heated (1); flat section at boiling point — temperature constant while boiling (1); temperature rises as gas is heated (1) — any four.

question: A 2 kg block of iron is heated from 20°C to 120°C using a 100 W heater. The specific heat capacity of iron is 450 J/kg°C. Calculate the energy needed and the time the heater must be on.

A gas in a rigid container has a pressure of 150 kPa at 300 K. The container is heated until the pressure reaches 250 kPa. Calculate the new temperature and explain the change in terms of particle behaviour.
mark_scheme: P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂ → 150/300 = 250/T₂ (1); T₂ = 500 K (1); particles have more kinetic energy at higher temperature (1); collide more frequently and with greater force increasing pressure (1).

question: Explain the difference between evaporation and boiling. Include how temperature, location and energy are involved in each process.
mark_scheme: Evaporation occurs at the surface of a liquid (1); can occur at any temperature below boiling point (1); fastest particles escape from surface (1). Boiling occurs throughout the liquid (1); only at the boiling point (1); requires continuous energy input (1); temperature stays constant during boiling (1) — any five.

question: A student conducts an experiment to find the specific heat capacity of aluminium. They heat a 1 kg block with a 50 W heater for 10 minutes and record a temperature rise of 62°C. Evaluate the experiment, calculate the specific heat capacity and explain why it differs from the accepted value of 900 J/kg°C.
mark_scheme: E = Pt = 50 × 600 = 30 000 J (1); c = E/(mΔT) = 30 000 ÷ (1 × 62) (1) = 484 J/kg°C (1); this is lower than 900 J/kg°C (1); because energy was lost to surroundings / not all energy went into the block (1); could improve by insulating the block / using a lid (1); thermometer may not have been in best position (1) — any six.

question: Explain how the particle model accounts for gas pressure, and how changes in temperature and volume affect pressure. Include reference to absolute zero in your answer.
mark_scheme: Gas particles move randomly and collide with container walls (1); each collision exerts a force — total force per unit area is pressure (1); increasing temperature increases kinetic energy of particles (1); more frequent and harder collisions increase pressure (1); decreasing volume means same particles in smaller space (1); more frequent collisions increase pressure (1); at absolute zero particles have minimum kinetic energy (1); gas pressure would theoretically be zero at 0 K (1) — any six.

question: An object has a mass of 8.1 kg and dimensions 30 cm × 15 cm × 20 cm. Calculate its volume in m³ and its density in kg/m³.
mark_scheme: Volume = 0.30 × 0.15 × 0.20 = 0.009 m³ (1); density = mass/volume = 8.1/0.009 (1) = 900 kg/m³ (1); correct unit stated (1).

question: Explain the differences in the arrangement and movement of particles in solids, liquids and gases. Explain why gases are much less dense than solids.
mark_scheme: Solid: particles in fixed positions, closely packed, regular arrangement, vibrating (1); liquid: particles close but able to move past each other, no fixed positions (1); gas: particles far apart, moving randomly at high speed (1); gases less dense because particles far apart — much more space between them than in solids (1).

question: Explain why sweating cools the body. Include reference to evaporation, latent heat and the kinetic energy of particles.
mark_scheme: Sweat (water) on skin evaporates (1); the faster-moving molecules escape from the surface (1); energy transferred from skin to water molecules to provide latent heat of vaporisation (1); this reduces the average kinetic energy of remaining skin molecules — skin cools (1).

question: Calculate the total energy needed to convert 200 g of ice at 0°C into steam at 100°C. Specific latent heat of fusion = 334 000 J/kg; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg°C; specific latent heat of vaporisation = 2 260 000 J/kg.
A bicycle tyre is pumped up on a cold morning. Explain, using kinetic theory, why the tyre pressure increases when the bike is ridden and the tyre warms up.
mark_scheme: Gas particles inside tyre move faster when temperature increases (1); particles collide with tyre walls more frequently (1); collisions are with greater force (1); greater force per unit area = higher pressure (1).

question: Describe how you would measure the density of a liquid, such as oil, in the laboratory. Include all measurements and calculations needed.
mark_scheme: Measure mass of empty measuring cylinder using balance (1); pour known volume of liquid into cylinder and measure mass again (1); mass of liquid = total mass − mass of empty cylinder (1); density = mass/volume — calculate with correct values and units (1).

question: Explain what is meant by internal energy. Explain what happens to internal energy and temperature when a substance is (a) heated as a solid and (b) melting.
mark_scheme: Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all particles in the substance (1); (a) heating solid: internal energy increases, kinetic energy of particles increases, temperature rises (1); (b) melting: energy supplied increases potential energy of particles as bonds are broken (1); kinetic energy does not increase so temperature stays constant (1).

question: A gas at 20°C has a pressure of 120 kPa. It is heated at constant volume until the pressure reaches 180 kPa. Calculate the new temperature in both kelvin and degrees Celsius.
Explain what Brownian motion is and how it provides evidence for the particle model. Describe the original experiment that demonstrated it.
mark_scheme: Brownian motion: random, erratic movement of small visible particles (1); e.g. pollen in water / smoke particles in air (1); caused by collisions with smaller, invisible molecules (1); provides evidence that matter is made of small, moving particles (1).

question: A piece of wood floats with half its volume submerged in water (density 1000 kg/m³). The wood has a volume of 0.004 m³. Calculate the mass and density of the wood.
mark_scheme: Volume submerged = 0.002 m³ (1); upthrust = weight of water displaced = 0.002 × 1000 × 10 = 20 N (1); since floating, weight of wood = 20 N; mass = 20/10 = 2 kg (1); density of wood = 2/0.004 = 500 kg/m³ (1).

question: Explain the difference between boiling and evaporation at the particle level. Why does evaporation cause cooling but boiling does not cool a substance below its boiling point?
mark_scheme: Evaporation: occurs at the surface at any temperature; only the fastest particles escape (1); as fastest particles leave, average kinetic energy of remaining particles decreases — temperature falls (1); boiling: occurs throughout liquid at boiling point (1); energy input maintains temperature at boiling point — temperature stays constant while boiling (1).

question: Explain, using kinetic theory, what would happen to the pressure of a fixed amount of gas if (a) the volume is halved at constant temperature, (b) the temperature is doubled at constant volume. Support with calculations using P₁ = 100 kPa, V₁ = 2 L, T₁ = 300 K.
mark_scheme: (a) P₁V₁ = P₂V₂: 100 × 2 = P₂ × 1; P₂ = 200 kPa (1); smaller volume means more frequent collisions with walls (1); (b) P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂: 100/300 = P₂/600; P₂ = 200 kPa (1); higher temperature means particles have more kinetic energy (1); more frequent and harder collisions with walls increase pressure (1).

question: Evaluate the suitability of water versus sand as a material to absorb and release thermal energy in a solar energy storage system. Use specific heat capacities (water c = 4200 J/kg°C, sand c = 800 J/kg°C).
mark_scheme: Water has much higher specific heat capacity than sand (1); water can store more energy per kg per degree (1); e.g. 1 kg water stores 4200 J/°C vs 800 J/°C for sand — water stores 5× more (1); water better for absorbing large amounts of solar energy with small temperature change (1); sand heats up quickly but stores less energy — releases heat quickly (1).

question: Explain in detail what happens to the particles and energy when steam at 100°C condenses to form water. Include reference to internal energy, kinetic energy and the forces between particles.
mark_scheme: Steam particles have high kinetic energy moving randomly at high speed (1); as steam cools, particles lose kinetic energy (1); at condensation point, particles slow enough for intermolecular forces to pull them together (1); potential energy decreases as bonds form between molecules (1); internal energy decreases — latent heat released to surroundings (1).

question: Describe how the densities of solids, liquids and gases compare and explain these differences using the particle model. Include a worked example comparing ice, water and steam.
mark_scheme: Solids: particles closely and regularly packed — high density (1); liquids: similar particle spacing to solids but slight increase — similar density to solids (1); gases: particles far apart — very low density (1); e.g. ice ~917 kg/m³, water ~1000 kg/m³ — close because particles similar spacing (1); steam ~0.6 kg/m³ — very low because particles far apart (1).

question: A gas occupies 3.0 L at a pressure of 200 kPa and a temperature of 27°C. Calculate the volume when the temperature is raised to 127°C and the pressure is reduced to 100 kPa.

A student heats 0.5 kg of water from 20°C to 100°C and then converts it all to steam. Calculate (a) the energy to heat the water (c = 4200 J/kg°C) and (b) the energy to vaporise it (L = 2 260 000 J/kg). Explain why so much more energy is needed for vaporisation.
mark_scheme: E₁ = mcΔT = 0.5 × 4200 × 80 = 168 000 J (1); E₂ = mL = 0.5 × 2 260 000 = 1 130 000 J (1); vaporisation requires ~6.7× more energy than heating (1); because during vaporisation, bonds between all molecules must be completely broken (1); much greater separation of particles required — far greater increase in potential energy (1).

question: Describe the particle model of a gas and use it to explain all three of the following observations: (a) gases fill their containers, (b) gases can be compressed, (c) gases exert pressure on container walls.
mark_scheme: Gas particles move randomly in all directions at high speed (1); (a) particles travel in straight lines until collision — they naturally fill all available space (1); (b) large spaces between particles allow them to be pushed closer together — gases are compressible (1); (c) particles collide with walls — each collision exerts a force (1); many collisions per second produce a net force per unit area = pressure (1).

question: Evaluate the evidence that temperature stays constant during a change of state. Describe an experiment, sketch the expected results and explain what the data shows about energy and particle behaviour.
mark_scheme: Experiment: heat ice in beaker from −10°C to 110°C at constant rate, record temperature every minute (1); expected graph: temperature rises, flat section at 0°C (melting), rises again, flat section at 100°C (boiling), rises (1); flat sections show temperature constant despite continuous energy input (1); energy used to break bonds between particles not to increase kinetic energy (1); confirms energy absorbed as latent heat during state change (1).

question: Explain the significance of absolute zero and what it means physically for gas particles. Explain why it is impossible to cool anything below absolute zero.
mark_scheme: Absolute zero = −273°C = 0 K (1); at absolute zero, particles have minimum possible kinetic energy (1); in theory, gas pressure would be zero at 0 K (1); impossible to go below because that would mean negative kinetic energy (1); cannot have less than zero kinetic energy — particles cannot move less than not at all (1).

question: A 0.5 kg metal is heated from 20°C to 70°C by a 100 W heater in 250 seconds. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal, compare it to aluminium (c = 900 J/kg°C) and suggest an identity for the metal from the data.
mark_scheme: E = Pt = 100 × 250 = 25 000 J (1); c = E/(mΔT) = 25 000/(0.5 × 50) (1) = 1000 J/kg°C (1); value close to iron (~450) or water (~4200) — likely not these (1); c = 1000 J/kg°C is close to glass/granite; student should identify a plausible metal (1) — accept any well-reasoned answer.

question: Explain why icebergs float on water, why this is important for marine life, and calculate the fraction of an iceberg submerged (density of ice = 917 kg/m³, density of water = 1000 kg/m³).
mark_scheme: Ice less dense than water (917 < 1000 kg/m³) so it floats (1); fraction submerged = density of ice/density of water = 917/1000 = 0.917 (1); 91.7% submerged, only about 8.3% visible above water (1); ice layer insulates water below — allows marine life to survive in cold winters (1); if ice were denser than water, oceans would freeze from the bottom up destroying ecosystems (1).

question: Evaluate the method of using a calorimeter to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal. Include a description of the method, the sources of error and how results could be improved.
mark_scheme: Heat known mass of metal in boiling water — record temperature (1); transfer to insulated calorimeter containing known mass of water — record water temperature before and after (1); use E_gained_by_water = mcΔT to find energy transferred (1); assume energy lost by metal = energy gained by water; use to calculate metal's SHC (1); error: heat lost to surroundings during transfer (1); error: incomplete thermal equilibrium — some energy stays in calorimeter (1); improvement: insulate calorimeter better / correct for heat capacity of calorimeter (1) — any six.

question: Explain in detail what happens to a gas when it is compressed rapidly, such as in a bicycle pump. Include reference to work done, temperature change, particle behaviour and pressure. Predict whether the compression is isothermal or adiabatic in practice.
mark_scheme: Work done on gas by piston (1); kinetic energy of gas particles increases (1); temperature of gas rises (1); higher temperature particles collide more frequently and with greater force (1); pressure increases both because of compression and temperature rise (1); in practice compression is adiabatic (not isothermal) — happens too quickly for heat to escape (1).

question: Evaluate the use of water as a coolant in industrial processes. Consider its thermal properties, including specific heat capacity, latent heat of vaporisation, and compare it with oil as an alternative coolant.
mark_scheme: Water: high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg°C) — can absorb large amounts of energy per kg (1); high latent heat of vaporisation (2.26 MJ/kg) — effective when evaporation allowed (1); cheap and widely available (1); disadvantage: corrodes metals, conducts electricity — safety issue in some applications (1); oil: lower specific heat capacity (~2000 J/kg°C) — less effective per kg (1); does not corrode metals / electrical insulator (1); used where water unsuitable e.g. transformer cooling (1) — any six.

question: Explain how density can be used to identify unknown materials. Describe the method for measuring density of (a) a regular solid, (b) an irregular solid, and (c) a liquid. Give one source of error for each.
mark_scheme: (a) regular solid: measure dimensions with ruler, calculate volume; measure mass with balance; ρ = m/V (1); error: ruler measurement uncertainty in calculating volume (1); (b) irregular solid: measure mass; use water displacement to find volume (1); error: air bubbles trapped on surface giving wrong volume (1); (c) liquid: measure mass of empty container, add liquid of known volume, find mass of liquid; ρ = m/V (1); error: liquid left on sides of container when pouring (1).

question: Explain the particle model and how it accounts for the properties of each state of matter. Include reference to particle spacing, kinetic energy, forces between particles and compressibility.
mark_scheme: Solid: particles closely packed in regular arrangement, strong forces between particles (1); low kinetic energy — only vibration, cannot move past each other — fixed shape and volume (1); Liquid: similar spacing to solid, weaker forces — particles slide past each other (1); takes shape of container but has fixed volume — not easily compressed (1); Gas: particles far apart, negligible forces (1); high kinetic energy, move freely and rapidly — fills container, easily compressed (1).

question: Evaluate the risks and benefits of using pressurised gas in aerosol cans. Explain the physics of how they work and what safety precautions are needed.
mark_scheme: Aerosol contains liquid propellant under high pressure (1); pressure greater than atmospheric so gas pushes liquid out when valve opened (1); if can is heated, gas pressure increases (P ∝ T at constant volume) (1); if pressure exceeds can's strength, can explodes — hazard (1); benefit: convenient delivery of product in fine spray (1); safety: do not store near heat sources — temperature increases pressure (1); do not puncture — sudden release of high pressure can cause injury (1) — any six.

question: Explain, using the particle model and energy concepts, how freeze-drying food works. Include changes of state, pressure, latent heat and why this is better than conventional drying for preserving food quality.
mark_scheme: Food frozen — water turns to ice (1); pressure reduced to below triple point so ice sublimes directly to water vapour without melting (1); sublimation requires latent heat — absorbed from surroundings keeping food cold (1); water vapour removed by vacuum pump (1); low temperature prevents degradation of vitamins/flavour (1); conventional drying uses heat — damages nutrients and changes texture (1).

question: Evaluate the design of a hot air balloon. Explain the physics of why it rises, including reference to density, buoyancy and the gas laws. Discuss the factors a pilot must control to maintain altitude.
mark_scheme: Heating air in envelope increases temperature — particles move faster and some escape (1); remaining air has same volume but lower mass — density decreases (1); buoyancy (upthrust) = weight of air displaced; if envelope density < surrounding air density, balloon rises (1); pilot increases burner to heat air, increasing temperature further reducing density (1); to descend: allow air to cool or open vent — density increases (1); gas law: at constant pressure, volume ∝ temperature — envelope expands as heated (1).

question: State the equation for density and give the SI unit of density.
mark_scheme: Density = mass ÷ volume / ρ = m/V (1); unit: kg/m³ (1).

question: Give two differences between the arrangement of particles in a solid and a gas.
mark_scheme: Any two: solids have closely packed particles; gases have particles far apart (1); solids have particles in a regular arrangement; gas particles are randomly distributed (1); solids have particles that only vibrate; gas particles move rapidly and randomly in all directions (1).

question: Name the two types of energy that make up the internal energy of a substance.
mark_scheme: Kinetic energy (energy due to particle motion) (1); potential energy (energy due to forces between particles) (1).

question: State what is meant by specific latent heat of fusion.
mark_scheme: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance from solid to liquid (or liquid to solid) (1); without changing its temperature (1).

question: Describe how you would measure the density of a small, irregularly shaped stone.
mark_scheme: Measure the mass of the stone using a balance (1); measure the volume by water displacement — submerge in a measuring cylinder and read the volume of water displaced; calculate ρ = m/V (1).

question: Give the equation for calculating the energy needed to heat a substance and state what each variable represents.
mark_scheme: E = mcΔT (1); E = energy in J, m = mass in kg, c = specific heat capacity in J/kg°C, ΔT = temperature change in °C (1).

question: State what happens to the temperature of water as it is heated from solid ice to boiling water, including any periods where temperature does not change.
mark_scheme: Temperature rises as ice is heated (1); temperature stays constant at 0°C while ice melts; temperature rises again through 0°C to 100°C; stays constant at 100°C while water boils (1).

question: Give two ways in which the internal energy of a substance can be increased.
mark_scheme: Any two: heating the substance (1); doing work on the substance, e.g. compressing a gas (1); exothermic chemical reactions release energy increasing internal energy (1).

question: Describe what happens to the energy supplied to a substance and to its particles during melting.
mark_scheme: Energy supplied is used to break bonds between particles rather than to increase their kinetic energy (1); as a result the temperature does not rise — energy is stored as increased potential energy of the particles (1).

question: Name the change of state that occurs when a gas is cooled and turns directly into a solid, and give an example.
mark_scheme: Deposition (or reverse sublimation) (1); example: frost forming on a cold surface / carbon dioxide dry ice forming (1). Award credit for sublimation if student answers the reverse — solid to gas.

question: Explain, using the particle model, why gases have much lower densities than solids of the same substance.
mark_scheme: In a solid, particles are closely packed together in a regular arrangement (1); in a gas, the same particles are spread far apart with large empty spaces between them (1); because density = mass/volume, the same mass occupies a much larger volume in the gas state, giving a much lower density (1).

question: Describe the particle arrangement, movement and spacing in each of the three states of matter.
mark_scheme: Solid: closely packed, regular arrangement, particles only vibrate about fixed positions (1); liquid: particles close together but no fixed positions — can move past each other, slightly more disordered than solid (1); gas: particles far apart, moving rapidly and randomly in all directions, no fixed positions (1).

question: Explain what happens to the internal energy of a substance when it is heated as a solid, and then when it starts to melt.
mark_scheme: When heated as a solid, the kinetic energy of the particles increases — particles vibrate faster and internal energy increases (1); temperature rises as kinetic energy increases (1); during melting, energy supplied increases the potential energy of particles as bonds begin to break — kinetic energy does not increase so temperature stays constant while melting occurs (1).

question: Explain why water is used as a coolant in car engines. Include reference to its specific heat capacity.
mark_scheme: Water has a high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg°C) (1); this means it can absorb large amounts of thermal energy for a small rise in temperature (1); water is effective at carrying heat away from the engine without boiling, preventing overheating (1).

question: Describe an experiment to measure the specific latent heat of fusion of ice.
mark_scheme: Set up a funnel with ice and a heater — measure the mass of water collected in a known time with the heater on (1); repeat with heater off (same time) to account for melting from room temperature alone — subtract to find mass melted by heater alone (1); energy supplied by heater = P × t; L = E/m (1).

question: Compare the compressibility of solids, liquids and gases. Explain the difference in terms of particle spacing.
mark_scheme: Gases are highly compressible — large spaces between particles that can be reduced (1); liquids are almost incompressible — particles are already close together with little space between them (1); solids are virtually incompressible — particles are tightly packed in fixed positions; the strong forces between particles resist compression (1).

question: Explain why ice floats on water despite both being made of water molecules.
mark_scheme: Ice is less dense than liquid water (ice ≈ 917 kg/m³; water ≈ 1000 kg/m³) (1); when water freezes, the molecules form a hexagonal crystal structure that is less tightly packed than liquid water (1); because ice is less dense than water, the upthrust on it exceeds its weight, so it floats (1).

question: Explain why coastal areas have a more moderate climate than inland areas. Use the concept of specific heat capacity in your answer.
mark_scheme: Water has a much higher specific heat capacity than land (4200 J/kg°C vs ~800 J/kg°C for soil) (1); the sea absorbs large amounts of energy in summer with only a small temperature rise, and releases this energy slowly in winter (1); coastal areas are kept cooler in summer and warmer in winter by proximity to the sea — smaller temperature range than inland areas (1).

question: Describe the energy changes that occur when steam at 100°C condenses to liquid water.
mark_scheme: As steam condenses, energy is released — the latent heat of vaporisation is released to the surroundings (1); the potential energy of the particles decreases as bonds (intermolecular forces) form between molecules (1); during condensation, the temperature stays constant at 100°C — kinetic energy of the particles does not change until all the steam has condensed (1).

question: Compare the time taken to heat 1 kg of water and 1 kg of iron by 10°C using the same heater, given that c(water) = 4200 J/kg°C and c(iron) = 450 J/kg°C.
mark_scheme: Energy to heat water = 1 × 4200 × 10 = 42 000 J (1); energy to heat iron = 1 × 450 × 10 = 4500 J (1); water requires approximately 9.3 times more energy — it takes much longer to heat water than iron by the same temperature rise using the same heater (1).

question: Explain the difference between temperature and internal energy of a substance.
mark_scheme: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance (1); internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a substance (1); a large cold object can have more internal energy than a small hot object, because it has more particles even if each has lower average kinetic energy (1).

question: Describe how you would measure the density of a liquid in the laboratory. Include all measurements needed.
mark_scheme: Measure the mass of an empty measuring cylinder using a balance (1); pour a measured volume of liquid into the cylinder and record the volume; measure the total mass again (1); mass of liquid = total mass − mass of empty cylinder; calculate density = mass/volume with correct units (kg/m³ or g/cm³) (1).
